analysis.one_liner: Rewrites federal grazing rules to lock in ranchers' grazing rights, extend permits to 15 years, and limit environmental review.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 60 cosponsors, cleared a House subcommittee by voice vote in September 1995 but never reached the full House or Senate, and died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite how livestock grazing is managed on federal land run by the Interior Department. It would give ranchers permits lasting 15 years with first priority at renewal, attach their grazing rights to their private base property so the rights can be sold or used as loan collateral, and set grazing fees by a formula based on the gross value of livestock production. It would also prohibit any reduction in grazing levels authorized as of August 1993 and block extra environmental review of individual grazing permits.
analysis.who_benefits: Ranchers who hold federal grazing permits and leases gain the most: longer permits, first-priority renewal, transferable grazing rights attached to their private land, compensation for improvements if grazing is cancelled, and permission to pledge permits as loan security. Banks that lend to ranchers also gain a new form of collateral.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires grazing permits and leases to be issued for a 15-year term, and gives the permit holder first priority for renewal at the end of the term.
Grazing preference rights attach to the rancher's private base property and may be transferred with it, and permits may be pledged as security for loans.
The bill states that nothing in it may be construed to reduce the levels of livestock grazing authorized as of August 1, 1993.
The bill sets the grazing fee by a formula based on the gross value of livestock production derived from private grazing-lease rate data, replacing the existing fee formula and Executive Order.

The bill says a grazing permit consistent with a land use plan is not a federal action requiring any study or assessment under the National Environmental Policy Act, and that no environmental consideration beyond the land-use-plan studies is required.

If a permit is cancelled to devote the land to another public purpose, the rancher receives compensation at fair market value for permanent range improvements, and the bill directs cooperative agreements designed to give permit holders an incentive to invest in range improvements with title shared proportionally.

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the public would pay. Grazing fees set by a production-value formula, combined with locked-in grazing levels and no per-permit environmental review, would leave taxpayers covering the gap between what grazing costs the government to administer and what permit holders pay, while rangeland, wildlife habitat, and water on federal land would bear the effects of grazing that could not be reduced.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and users of federal rangeland

drawbacks.text: The bill bars any term or condition in a grazing permit beyond those it lists, and requires a reduction in grazing use to be implemented over up to five years with monitoring data, slowing action when rangeland is being damaged.
It removes National Grasslands and land utilization projects from the National Forest System, shifting their management purpose toward livestock grazing under the Bankhead-Jones Farm Tenant Act.

The bill's own findings declare that federal rangelands are in the best condition of the century and frame federal grazing policy around maintaining the economic viability of the western livestock industry, an assumption critics of subsidized grazing contest.

Federal grazing fees have long been far below comparable private grazing rates, and any fee formula that anchors to production value risks keeping the program running at a loss to taxpayers; the bill requires annual reporting of grazing revenues and costs, implicitly acknowledging the accounting question.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 20,000 western ranchers who hold federal grazing permits, this bill would have been a substantial win: longer, more secure permits, transferable rights usable as collateral, and compensation protections. For the public, the costs are the subsidy gap between fees and administration costs, the removal of environmental review for individual permits, and the statutory floor preventing reductions in grazing even when monitoring shows damage. The bill does include real enforcement provisions against unauthorized grazing, but its center of gravity is entrenching the existing grazing operations, not reforming them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill got hearings and a subcommittee vote in 1995, but the full Natural Resources Committee never voted on it and the House floor never saw it; the action history points readers to a companion Senate bill, and neither became law before the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 25, 1995 by Rep. Wes Cooley with 27 original cosponsors and referred jointly to the Resources and Agriculture Committees.
It gathered 60 cosponsors, 51 Republicans and 9 Democrats.
A subcommittee held hearings on July 11, 1995, and on September 12, 1995 forwarded an amended version to the full committee by voice vote.
The full committee never took it up and the House never voted on it; the April 1996 action entry says further action is found in the Senate companion S.1459.
No version of the legislation became law before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal rangelands stayed under existing law, so conservation and recreation users of public land and taxpayers avoided the new entitlements the bill would have given grazing permit holders. Western ranchers and their lenders gained nothing from this Congress.

for.name: Rep. Wes Cooley
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and organized 27 original cosponsors for its introduction.

for.name: 51 of 60 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it broad House support on paper.

against.name: Clinton administration (Interior Department)

against.what_they_did: Campaigned against grazing legislation that would entrench rancher preferences and limit environmental review of federal rangeland management.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily Republican — 51 of 60 — though 9 Democrats signed on, and the bill's steepest obstacles came from committee inaction and Senate-side politics rather than a floor vote.

industries.industry: Federal-land livestock ranchers (cattle and sheep permit holders)
industries.note: The bill would lock in their grazing preferences on federal land, grant 15-year permits with renewal priority, let the rights transfer with private base property and serve as loan collateral, and bar reductions below 1993 levels. Ranchers already pay far less to graze federal land than comparable private rates, so every entrenchment provision is a public subsidy to a small, concentrated group.
By letting grazing permits be pledged as loan security, the bill would create a new form of federally backed collateral, shifting risk toward the public land base that secures private loans.

industries.industry: Public-lands recreation, wildlife, and conservation interests
industries.note: The bill would prevent reductions in grazing levels even where monitoring shows damage, remove per-permit environmental review, and shift National Grasslands toward livestock-grazing purposes — reducing the standing of non-grazing users of federal rangeland.
